Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Alexandria Pizz 
General Comment
From:
Alexandria Pizza
Visual/Graphic Designer
Coral Springs, FL
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI-RFI-2025-4493.rationale: The commenter argues that AI training uses copyrighted work without consent or compensation and urges against new copyright exemptions, plus calls for transparency and labeling—captured as copyright/IP and consumer-harm-related concerns. General Comment
The conversation around AI and it's role in our daily lives is embarrassing. I work in the creative industries as a comics editor and writer. I
come across copyright every day in my work--from acquiring titles and filing copyrights with creators, to making sure that copyrights are
printed correctly on work for the sake of individuals and companies, to having to know what exists under copyright and what is already in

doesn't make money. They've also said that they won't make a profit, unless they're allowed to dismantle our copyright system for their

in the process of many legal proceedings already, admitted to intellectual property theft. Many systems have had to be shut down for
giving misleading information--both the inconvenient, like systems that were practically giving away cars, and the dangerous, that provided
inaccurate and harmful medical information. Consumer trust goes down when AI are added to systems, in large part due to the
inaccuracies. 
Simply put, our AI Action Plan should be complete divestment. America doesn't need to be the leader in a scam that, again, so far doesn't
even accomplish it's goal of making the wealthy wealthier. To develop a plan to infringe upon copyright, privacy, and the interests of
businesses both large and small is shameful.

From:
Mal Pietsch
Sleepy Hollow, New York
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who has always wanted to make a career out of art. I have been lucky enough to have the space and time to
practice and create and develop a niche for myself, and I am friends with many other creatives who have gone far enough to make careers
out of art. This measure is a threat to all of us.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like those run by my friends and loved ones with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of hundreds of thousands of everyday American
creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then
sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Name: Michael Stackpole 
General Comment
See attached file(s)
Attachments
AI carve out Note

From:
Michael A. Stackpole
New York Times Bestselling author of over 70 novels, award winning 
novelist, graphic novelist, game designer, computer game designer, 
podcaster, editor and screenwriter
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the 
Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am a self-employed American entrepreneur in the entertainment 
industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and 
knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make 
a decent living—and planned to continue doing so into the future. 
This plan seemed good until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI 
(Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American 
small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by 
people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of 
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our 
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly 
competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create 
exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American 
creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a 
machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use.” 
By this turn of logic, the fact that a thief steals my wallet means that my 
wallet is instantly transformed into “community property” owned by 
everybody.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – 
regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim 

that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this 
way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American 
copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we 
put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to 
create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new visual design, a new, blockbuster novel; or a new 
piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and 
Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly 
make a living doing these things? 
And, as a writer, I have to say, the sheer gall and irony of people 
advocating for their opportunity to make money in a “free market” 
environment while stealing from others is incredibly rich. Which is what 
exactly they mean to be by depriving any of the rest of us from attaining 
that goal. 
Thing about the above paragraph is that my point is made through a 
pun—the dual meanings of rich in our tongue. And no matter how well 
they fine tune their LLMs, AI will never be able to make a point that way. 
Why? Because the effect of that pun hinges on the reader’s emotional 
reaction to that pun. These machines can’t do puns because they have 
no emotions. 
And granting them the right to use our work without payment, through 
these carveouts means that they’re cutting off the only source of fuel 
they have. Before long the only thing AI will mine is drivel generated by 
AI. Their model is unsustainable regardless of the carveouts, but 
granting those carveouts hurts writers, artists, programmers, musicians 
and other human beings. The cost of giving in to their demand is the 
slow death of human culture and art. 
Want to protect American innovation, American culture and our soul? 
Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions 
that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators 
and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or 
transparency.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away 
creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair 
marketplace with competition:
•
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday 
Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when 
and where our work is used by AI systems. 
•
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing 
marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is 
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value 
generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not 
just Big Tech. 
•
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big 
Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in 
their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated. 
I am not anti-technology nor anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the 
capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for 
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where

our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

comment

 

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we 
put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to 
create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to 
have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating 
it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these 
things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do 
not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech 
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away 
creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair 
marketplace with competition:
	 •	
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday 
Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when 
and where our work is used by AI systems.
	 •	
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing 
marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is 
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value 
generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not 
just Big Tech.
	 •	
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big 
Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in 
their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the 
capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for 
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting 
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

White House AI Action Plan Comment Letter

March 14, 2025 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

They also raise harms to small businesses/consumers via unfair competition and lack of transparency, aligning with consumer harm concerns. The submission is from an anonymous individual (no organization affiliation).

I am an everyday American who has worked in marketing, graphic design, web design, and 
illustration. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my 
business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living, but recent changes in the 
creative landscape of my fields threatens to change this. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses and freelancers with their 
recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Letter

March 15, 2025 
From: 
Tia Greenlee 
Data Analysts and Illustrator 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

The AI Action Plan should focus... on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition... require transparency... disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

They also raise harms to creators and small businesses and request transparency/labeling, which aligns with consumer harm concerns. Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Joshua Fink
General Comment
Any AI that requires the theft of intellectual property in order to succeed is completely and utterly unethical. This is not a matter of
American superiority in AI, it's a matter of American businessmen wanting to further maximize their profits by replacing skilled American
workers with automated replacements. The only people that are uplifted by this is the already wealthy, and provides no benefit for the rest
of the country. It, in fact, will only harm them and thus this cannot be allowed to pass.
If an AI system requires training to succeed, it should be on material that has naturally entered the public domain or has been approved to
be used by the creators of the material - preferably with some manner of reimbursement to the latter for their assistance. An opt-in
approach rather than an opt-out, and should 100% be held to by the law to only use this material rather than giving private companies
carte blanche to steal intellectual property - American or otherwise. This would allow the American populace and foreign allies to assist in
the improvement of AI development and be properly rewarded for their efforts rather than having their work stolen from them.
In addition, the environmental and energy issues caused by such training need to also be monitored and addressed. Any development
should and must include attempts to limit the amount of energy used and the harm it causes to the environment in line with any other
preexisting laws and agreements - and perhaps should require additional rules and oversight specific to mitigate its damages.
Circumventing these will similarly cause more harm than good to the United States.
If a system cannot function without theft of intellectual property and unnecessary amounts of harm to our country's resources and
environment, then that is its own failing and thus should fail. It should not be propped up and granted special privilege to perpetuate its
crimes and damage in order to succeed. It imposes and hinders the freedoms and rights of the American populace - past, present, and
future. Because while there are already many ways letting this pass will cause immediate harm, there's potential for this ruling to set a
precedent that will further impinge upon and reduce the freedoms and the rights of US citizens in the future.
The only correct way to move forward with this - if it should be allowed to do so at all - is with appropriate oversight and laws in place in
order to protect the creative liberties and intellectual property of the American populace and its foreign allies, as well as the health and
safety of the nation's resources and environment if not the world as whole. Not further elevate only the wealthy and further reinforce the
idea that laws and rules do not apply to them, as that only further weakens and harms our nation as a whole.

If an AI system requires training to succeed, it should be on material that has naturally entered the public domain or has been approved to be used by the creators... In addition, the environmental and energy issues caused by such training need to also be monitored and addressed... perhaps should require additional rules and oversight specific to mitigate its damages.

Public Comment on AI Copywrite

March 14, 2025
From:
S.E.Clark
Writer and Artist
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who writes short stories and teaches creative writing for a living. I have 
worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky 
enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy 
thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs 
in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the 
work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it 
back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to 
make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting 
that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should 
be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in 
this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate. 

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new piece of literature, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we 
possibly make a living doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans 
without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so 
that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to 
create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated 
by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to 
disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, 
and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds 
of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
